paras.text: The global decrease in stratospheric ozone is correlated with rising level of chlorine and bromine in the stratosphere from the manufacture and release of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other halocarbons. paras.text: The quality of water is very important because of its role in human health and benefits of aquatic ecosystem. Water pollution is any change in the physical chemical or biological properties of water that will have harmful effects on humans, environment and ecosystem. Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies (lakes, oceans, seas, rivers, and groundwater) usually caused by the human activities, agricultural, industrial, mining and other activities.

paras.text: Some of the water pollution is caused by direct sources, such as factories, waste management facilities, refineries etc. that directly release waste and harmful by-products into the nearest water source. Indirect sources include pollutants that enter the water bodies via ground water or soil or via the atmosphere as acid rain. Discharge of sewage from homes and commercial establishments, reduces the dissolved oxygen content, again upsetting the biological balance of surface water. All of these activities make water unfit for drinking and public use. Such water is said to be polluted water which needs treatment before it is made fit for public use.

paras.text: Two sub-categories of the undissolved solid material present in water can be recognized. One consists of particles large enough to be removed by running the water through a filtering apparatus. The second, consists of particles so small that they cannot be removed by such treatments. Those in the second category are called colloids, which are too small to be seen, even with a microscope. They can, however, be detected, because they give water a turbid or cloudy appearance. They are most easily detected by passing a beam of light through the water and observing the scattering of light they produce like a beam of light passing through smoky or foggy air.

paras.text: The dissolved solid material, present in water, may either be organic or inorganic. The dissolved organic compounds, acting as impurities, enter into water as a result of the growth and the death of aquatic plants, such as algae. Others are contributed by sewage from domestic sewage systems and by industrial wastes. The combined total amount of all the organic and inorganic substances found in water are represented by a term, “total dissolved solids” (TDS). 23.3 Water Pollution and Water Treatment

The quality of water is very important because of its role in human health and benefits of aquatic ecosystem. Water pollution is any change in the physical chemical or biological properties of water that will have harmful effects on humans, environment and ecosystem. Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies (lakes, oceans, seas, rivers, and groundwater) usually caused by the human activities, agricultural, industrial, mining and other activities.

Some of the most commonly occurring water pollutants are:

Domestic waste

Insecticides and pesticides.

Industrial effluents.

Detergents and fertilizers.

Some of the water pollution is caused by direct sources, such as factories, waste management facilities, refineries etc. that directly release waste and harmful by-products into the nearest water source. Indirect sources include pollutants that enter the water bodies via ground water or soil or via the atmosphere as acid rain. Discharge of sewage from homes and commercial establishments, reduces the dissolved oxygen content, again upsetting the biological balance of surface water. All of these activities make water unfit for drinking and public use. Such water is said to be polluted water which needs treatment before it is made fit for public use.

Water that we either use or discard generally contains the following categories of undesirable substances (pollutants).

1. Suspended Solids and Sediments

Two sub-categories of the undissolved solid material present in water can be recognized. One consists of particles large enough to be removed by running the water through a filtering apparatus. The second, consists of particles so small that they cannot be removed by such treatments. Those in the second category are called colloids, which are too small to be seen, even with a microscope. They can, however, be detected, because they give water a turbid or cloudy appearance. 23.3 Water Pollution and Water Treatment

The quality of water is very important because of its role in human health and benefits of aquatic ecosystem. Water pollution is any change in the physical chemical or biological properties of water that will have harmful effects on humans, environment and ecosystem. Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies (lakes, oceans, seas, rivers, and groundwater) usually caused by the human activities, agricultural, industrial, mining and other activities.

Some of the most commonly occurring water pollutants are:

Domestic waste

Insecticides and pesticides.

Industrial effluents.

Detergents and fertilizers.

Some of the water pollution is caused by direct sources, such as factories, waste management facilities, refineries etc. that directly release waste and harmful by-products into the nearest water source. Indirect sources include pollutants that enter the water bodies via ground water or soil or via the atmosphere as acid rain. Discharge of sewage from homes and commercial establishments, reduces the dissolved oxygen content, again upsetting the biological balance of surface water. All of these activities make water unfit for drinking and public use. Such water is said to be polluted water which needs treatment before it is made fit for public use.

23.3.1 Types of Water Pollutants

Water that we either use or discard generally contains the following categories of undesirable substances (pollutants).

1. Suspended Solids and Sediments

Two sub-categories of the undissolved solid material present in water can be recognized. One consists of particles large enough to be removed by running the water through a filtering apparatus. The second, consists of particles so small that they cannot be removed by such treatments. Those in the second category are called colloids, which are too small to be seen, even with a microscope. They can, however, be detected, because they give water a turbid or cloudy appearance. They are most easily detected by passing a beam of light through the water and observing the scattering of light they produce like a beam of light passing through smoky or foggy air.

2. Dissolved Solids

The dissolved solid material, present in water, may either be organic or inorganic. The dissolved organic compounds, acting as impurities, enter into water as a result of the growth and the death of aquatic plants, such as algae. Others are contributed by sewage from domestic sewage systems and by industrial wastes. The combined total amount of all the organic and inorganic substances found in water are represented by a term, “total dissolved solids” (TDS). The dissolved inorganic materials present in water are mostly salts.
